paragraphs.heading: One equation for a gas
paragraphs.text: The ideal gas law links the main measurable properties of a gas in a single equation, pV = nRT. In it, p stands for pressure, V for volume and T for temperature, while n is the amount of substance and R is a fixed number called the ideal gas constant. For a given amount of gas, its pressure, volume and temperature together settle what state it is in.

paragraphs.heading: Units and the constant
paragraphs.text: The temperature in the equation has to be an absolute temperature, counted in kelvins. The Kelvin scale is the Celsius scale shifted so that 0 K sits at −273.15 °C, the lowest temperature possible. In SI units, pressure goes in pascals, volume in cubic metres and amount in moles. R then has the value 8.314 J/(mol·K). The same constant can be written as 0.0821 L⋅atm/(mol⋅K), or roughly 2 cal/(mol·K).

paragraphs.heading: Counting particles instead
paragraphs.text: The modern equation comes in two main forms. One of them uses N, the number of particles in the gas, which are usually atoms or molecules. It also brings in the Boltzmann constant, k_B = 1.38×10⁻²³ J⋅K⁻¹. Written this way, the law says PV/NT = k_B.

paragraphs.heading: Why it works
paragraphs.text: The kinetic theory of ideal gases assumes that the atoms or molecules feel no pull toward one another. That means the gas has no potential energy, so all of its energy is the kinetic energy of its moving particles. August Krönig in 1856 and Rudolf Clausius in 1857 each derived the ideal gas law from this picture, working separately.

paragraphs.heading: Built from simpler laws
paragraphs.text: The older laws behind this equation came from experiments that changed just two properties of a gas and held all the others fixed. Boyle, for example, kept both the number of particles and the temperature constant. Since each of these rules holds only while the other properties stay put, you cannot just merge them with algebra. Any derivation has to keep track of what each experiment held constant.

paragraphs.heading: Where it falls short
paragraphs.text: The equation applies exactly only to an ideal gas, and otherwise serves as an approximation for real gases that act enough like one. It ignores both the size of the molecules and their pull on each other, so it works best for monatomic gases at high temperatures and low pressures. At low density, the gaps between molecules are much larger than the molecules, so their size matters less. At higher temperatures, the extra energy of motion makes the attractions matter less. Fuller equations, such as the van der Waals equation, allow for both effects.

paragraphs.heading: A telling example
paragraphs.text: When an ideal gas expands freely, its molecules do not interact and its temperature stays the same. In a real gas, molecules do attract or repel each other, depending on temperature and pressure, and the gas does warm or cool. This is called the Joule–Thomson effect. For air at room temperature and sea level, its coefficient μ_JT is 0.22 °C/bar.
